issues.legal_issue: In a suit in which the plaintiff may value the relief for court-fee purposes, the value chosen for court fees determines the value for jurisdiction, rather than the jurisdictional value determining the court-fee value.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought partition of alleged joint-family property and an account.
The plaint stated a value for jurisdiction but did not specifically state the value of the partition relief for court-fee purposes.
The court determined that the partition claim fell under the provision allowing the plaintiff to value the relief, and the plaintiff then valued that relief separately.
issues.conclusion: The plaintiff’s chosen value for the relief for court-fee purposes determines the jurisdictional value; the jurisdictional valuation stated earlier cannot itself be treated as the court-fee valuation.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 7(iv)(b) of the Court-Fees Act, 1870, the plaintiff states the value of the relief sought in a suit to enforce a right to share in property on the ground that it is joint-family property. Section 8 of the Suits Valuation Act, 1887, makes the value for jurisdiction the same as the value determinable for court fees. The court-fee value is primary, and the jurisdictional value follows from it.

predicates.partition_or_share_claim: The plaintiff seeks partition or enforcement of a share in property claimed to be joint-family property.
predicates.plaintiff_may_choose_relief_value: The kind of relief claimed is one for which the plaintiff is permitted to state the value of the relief.
predicates.plaintiff_states_court_fee_value: The plaintiff states a value for the relief for the purpose of calculating court fees.

issues.definition: When a plaintiff states a court-fee value for a claim whose value the plaintiff may choose, the jurisdictional value follows that stated value.

issues.legal_issue: When a plaintiff has not specifically valued a relief for court-fee purposes and the court determines that the claim is one for which the plaintiff may state its value, the plaintiff should ordinarily be allowed to amend the plaint to state that value.
material_facts: The plaintiff initially paid a fixed fee for the partition relief and did not specify its value for court-fee purposes.
The court determined that the relief was governed by a provision permitting the plaintiff to state its value.
The plaintiff sought permission to amend the plaint to state the value he assigned to the relief.
issues.conclusion: The plaintiff should be allowed to amend the plaint to state the value of the relief for court-fee purposes, rather than being held to the jurisdictional value previously stated.
issues.legal_principle: Section 7(iv)(b) of the Court-Fees Act, 1870, requires the plaintiff to state the amount at which the relief is valued. Read with section 8 of the Suits Valuation Act, 1887, the stated court-fee value determines the jurisdictional value. The court relied on the Full Bench decision in Karam Ilahi v. Muhammad Bashir, AIR 1949 Lahore 116, in supporting the ordinary allowance of an amendment where the court-fee valuation was omitted.

predicates.suit_with_plaintiff_valued_relief: The proceeding is a suit in which the plaintiff is entitled to state the value of the relief claimed.
predicates.court_fee_value_omitted: The plaint does not specifically state the value of the relief for court-fee purposes.
predicates.jurisdiction_value_stated: The plaint states a value for jurisdiction without specifying a court-fee value for the relief.

issues.definition: If a plaintiff in a suit with a plaintiff-valued relief omits its court-fee value but states a jurisdictional value, the plaintiff should ordinarily be allowed to amend the plaint to state the court-fee value.

issues.legal_issue: The statutory power to examine the sufficiency of court fees on a plaint and appeal applies to proceedings on the original side when the applicable court rules extend the court-fee law in other respects.
material_facts: The suit and subsequent appeal arose on the original side of the High Court.
The High Court Fees Rules applied the court-fee law to specified documents and, for other documents including memoranda of appeal, extended that law in every other respect.
The Division Bench considered whether the court fees paid on the plaint and appeal were sufficient.
issues.conclusion: The Division Bench could exercise the statutory power to examine the adequacy of court fees on the plaint and appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Section 12(1) and (2) of the Court-Fees Act, 1870, provides for decisions on proper court fees and empowers an appellate, reference, or revisional court to examine whether the proper fee was paid on the plaint. Order II, rule 1 of the Madras High Court Fees Rules, 1933, extended the court-fee law to other documents, including memoranda of appeal, in every other respect. The court held that this extension included the power under section 12.

predicates.original_side_proceeding: The suit or appeal is proceeding on the original side of a High Court.
predicates.court_rules_extend_fee_law_to_other_docu: Applicable court rules extend the court-fee law to other documents, including appeals, in respects beyond the specified fees and their levy.
predicates.fee_sufficiency_in_plaint_or_appeal_is_c: The court is asked to determine whether the proper court fee was paid on the plaint or appeal.

issues.definition: When an original-side proceeding is subject to court rules extending the court-fee law to other documents and fee sufficiency is considered, the court may review the fee paid.

issues.legal_issue: A judge’s decision under the statutory procedure for resolving court-fee disputes is not final when the record does not establish that the judge was appointed by the Chief Justice to exercise that authority.
material_facts: A dispute about the court fee payable on an original-side plaint was referred to a judge sitting in chambers.
The record did not establish that the Chief Justice had appointed that judge, generally or specially, to decide such disputes.
A later Division Bench therefore considered whether the earlier decision was final.
issues.conclusion: The earlier decision was not final under the statutory procedure because the record did not establish the required appointment.
issues.legal_principle: Section 5 of the Court-Fees Act, 1870, makes a decision final when the dispute is decided by the Chief Justice or a High Court judge appointed by the Chief Justice, generally or specially, for that purpose. The court declined to infer an appointment from the asserted practice of the High Court when the record contained no evidence of one.

predicates.court_fee_dispute_reference: A dispute between a suitor and the court office about the necessity or amount of a court fee is referred for decision.
predicates.judge_decides_as_chamber_judge: A judge sitting in chambers decides the referred court-fee dispute.
predicates.no_record_of_authorized_appointment: The record contains no evidence that the judge was appointed by the Chief Justice, generally or specially, to decide the dispute.

issues.definition: A chamber judge’s decision on a referred court-fee dispute is not final under the special procedure when the record does not show the judge’s authorized appointment.

issues.legal_issue: A court-fee classification decision made by an authorized judge in the statutory reference procedure is final and cannot be reopened in a later appeal.
material_facts: A Master referred the dispute about the fee on the appeal to a Division Bench pursuant to an order of the Chief Justice.
The Division Bench determined that the appeal was to be valued under the provision for enforcing a right to share in joint-family property.
The respondent’s argument that a different fee provision applied was not reopened in the Supreme Court.
issues.conclusion: The Division Bench’s determination of the court-fee classification was final, and the Supreme Court proceeded on the basis that the appeal was governed by the provision for plaintiff-valued relief.
issues.legal_principle: Section 5 of the Court-Fees Act, 1870, provides finality for a court-fee decision made by the Chief Justice or a judge appointed by the Chief Justice after a qualifying reference. The court held that the Division Bench’s decision pursuant to the requisite order was final, notwithstanding that the respondent had not been heard on that reference.

predicates.court_fee_dispute_reference: A dispute about the proper court fee is referred for decision through the prescribed court-fee procedure.
predicates.judge_authorized_by_chief_justice: The judge deciding the reference has been appointed or directed by the Chief Justice to decide it.
predicates.judge_decides_fee_classification: The judge determines which basis of court-fee valuation applies to the claim.

issues.definition: When an authorized judge decides the fee classification in a referred court-fee dispute, that classification decision is final.
